entries.1173b97a312195b4d7b665719c36ab9a4fe4f684: <div sID="gen6907" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="1Kgs.18" sID="1Kgs.18"/> <div eID="gen6907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6908" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6909" type="x-p"/> We left the prophet Elijah wrapt up in obscurity. It does not appear that either the increase of the provision or the raising of the child had caused him to be taken notice of at Zarephath, for then Ahab would have discovered him; he would rather do good than be known to do it. But in this chapter his appearance was as public as before his retirement was close; the days appointed for his concealment (which was part of the judgment upon Israel) being finished, he is now commanded to show himself to Ahab, and to expect rain upon the earth, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.1">ver. 1</reference>. Pursuant to this order we have here, I. His interview with Obadiah, one of Ahab's servants, by whom he sends notice to Ahab of his coming, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.2-1Kgs.18.16">ver. 2-16</reference>. II. His interview with Ahab himself, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17-1Kgs.18.20">ver. 17-20</reference>. III. His interview with all Israel upon Mount Carmel, in order to a public trial of titles between the Lord and Baal; a most distinguished solemnity it was, in which, 1. Baal and his prophets were confounded. 2. God and Elijah were honoured, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.21-1Kgs.18.39">ver. 21-39</reference>. IV. The execution he did upon the prophets of Baal, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.40">ver. 40</reference>. V. The return of the mercy of rain, at the word of Elijah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.41-1Kgs.18.46">ver. 41-46</reference>. It is a chapter in which are many things very observable.
entries.3108a02553e9bf079e6cf067b60b2c75335435f6: <div eID="gen6909" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6908" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of Obadiah; Elijah's Interview with Obadiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 906.)</title> <div sID="gen6910" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass <hi type="italic">after</hi> many days, that the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to Elijah in the third year, saying, Go, show thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Elijah went to show himself unto Ahab. And <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a sore famine in Samaria. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Ahab called Obadiah, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> the governor of <hi type="italic">his</hi> house. (Now Obadiah feared the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> greatly: <hi type="super">4</hi> For it was <hi type="italic">so,</hi> when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that Obadiah took a hundred prophets, and hid them by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water.) <hi type="super">5</hi> And Ahab said unto Obadiah, Go into the land, unto all fountains of water, and unto all brooks: peradventure we may find grass to save the horses and mules alive, that we lose not all the beasts. <hi type="super">6</hi> So they divided the land between them to pass throughout it: Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went another way by himself. <hi type="super">7</hi> And as Obadiah was in the way, behold, Elijah met him: and he knew him, and fell on his face, and said, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou that my lord Elijah? <hi type="super">8</hi> And he answered him, I <hi type="italic">am:</hi> go, tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah <hi type="italic">is here.</hi> <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said, What have I sinned, that thou wouldest deliver thy servant into the hand of Ahab, to slay me?   10 <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God liveth, there is no nation or kingdom, whither my lord hath not sent to seek thee: and when they said, <hi type="italic">He is</hi> not <hi type="italic">there;</hi> he took an oath of the kingdom and nation, that they found thee not. <hi type="super">11</hi> And now thou sayest, Go, tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah <hi type="italic">is here.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">as soon as</hi> I am gone from thee, that the Spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall carry thee whither I know not; and <hi type="italic">so</hi> when I come and tell Ahab, and he cannot find thee, he shall slay me: but I thy servant fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from my youth. <hi type="super">13</hi> Was it not told my lord what I did when Jezebel slew the prophets of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , how I hid a hundred men of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's prophets by fifty in a cave, and fed them with bread and water? <hi type="super">14</hi> And now thou sayest, Go, tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah <hi type="italic">is here:</hi> and he shall slay me. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Elijah said, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts liveth, before whom I stand, I will surely show myself unto him to day. <hi type="super">16</hi> So Obadiah went to meet Ahab, and told him: and Ahab went to meet Elijah. <div eID="gen6910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6911" type="x-p"/> In these verses we find, <div eID="gen6911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6912" type="x-p"/> I. The sad state of Israel at this time, upon two accounts:— <div eID="gen6912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6913" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">slew them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.13">v. 13</reference>. Being an idolater, she was a persecutor, and made Ahab one. Even in those bad times, when the calves were worshipped and the temple at Jerusalem deserted, yet there were some good people that feared God and served him, and some good prophets that instructed them in the knowledge of him and assisted them in their devotions. The priests and the Levites had all gone to Judah and Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.13-2Chr.11.14">2 Chron. xi. 13, 14</reference>), but, instead of them, God raised up these prophets, who read and expounded the law in private meetings, or in the families that retained their integrity, for we read not of any synagogues at this time; they had not the spirit of prophecy as Elijah, nor did they offer sacrifice, or burn incense, but taught people to live well, and keep close to the God of Israel. These Jezebel aimed to extirpate, and put many of them to death, which was as much a public calamity as a public iniquity, and threatened the utter ruin of religion's poor remains in Israel. Those few that escaped the sword were forced to abscond, and hide themselves in caves, where they were buried alive and cut off, though not from life, yet from usefulness, which is the end and comfort of life; and, when the prophets were persecuted and driven into corners, no doubt their friends, those few good people that were in the land, were treated in like manner. Yet, bad as things were, <div eID="gen6913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6914" type="x-p"/> (1.) There was one very good man, who was a great man at court, <hi type="italic">Obadiah,</hi> who answered his name—<hi type="italic">a servant of the Lord,</hi> one who feared God and was faithful to him, and yet was steward of the household to Ahab. Observe his character: He <hi type="italic">feared the Lord greatly</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.3">v. 3</reference>), was not only a good man, but zealously and eminently good; his great place put a lustre upon his goodness, and gave him great opportunities of doing good; and he <hi type="italic">feared the Lord from his youth</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.12">v. 12</reference>), he began betimes to be religious and had continued long. Note, Early piety, it is to be hoped, will be eminent piety; those that are good betimes are likely to be very good; he that feared God from his youth came to fear him greatly. He that will thrive must rise betimes. But it is strange to find such an eminently good man governor of Ahab's house, an office of great honour, power, and trust. [1.] It was strange that so wicked a man as Ahab would prefer him to it and continue him in it; certainly it was because he was a man of celebrated honesty, industry, and ingenuity, and one in whom he could repose a confidence, whose eyes he could trust as much as his own, as appears here, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.5">v. 5</reference>. Joseph and Daniel were preferred because there were none so fit as they for the places they were preferred to. Note, Those who profess religion should study to recommend themselves to the esteem even of those that are without by their integrity, fidelity, and application to business. [2.] It was strange that so good a man as Obadiah would accept of preferment in a court so addicted to idolatry and all manner of wickedness. We may be sure it was not made necessary to qualify him for preferment that he should be of the king's religion, that he should conform to the <hi type="italic">statues of Omri, or the law of the house of Ahab.</hi> Obadiah would not have accepted the place if he could not have had it without bowing the knee to Baal, nor was Ahab so impolitic as to exclude those from offices that were fit to serve him, merely because they would not join with him in his devotions. That man that is true to his God will be faithful to his prince. Obadiah therefore could with a good conscience enjoy the place, and therefore would not decline it, nor give it up, though he foresaw he could not do the good he desired to do in it. Those that fear God need not go out of the world, bad as it is. [3.] It was strange that either he did not reform Ahab or Ahab corrupt him; but it seems they were both fixed; he that was filthy would be filthy still, and he that was holy would be holy still. Those fear God greatly that keep up the fear of him in bad times and places; thus Obadiah did. God has his remnant among all sorts, high and low; there were saints in Nero's household, and in Ahab's. <div eID="gen6914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6915" type="x-p"/> (2.) This great good man used his power for the protection of God's prophets. He hid 100 of them in two caves, when the persecution was hot, and <hi type="italic">fed them with bread and water,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.4">v. 4</reference>. He did not think it enough to fear God himself, but, having wealth and power wherewith to do it, he thought himself obliged to assist and countenance others that feared God; nor did he think his being kind to them would excuse him from being good himself, but he did both, he both feared God greatly himself and patronised those that feared him likewise. See how wonderfully God raises up friends for his ministers and people, for their shelter in difficult times, even where one would least expect them. Bread and water were now scarce commodities, yet Obadiah will find a competence of both for God's prophets, to keep them alive for service hereafter, though now they were laid aside. <div eID="gen6915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6916" type="x-p"/> 2. When Jezebel cut off God's prophets God cut off the necessary provisions by the extremity of the drought. Perhaps Jezebel persecuted God's prophets under pretence that they were the cause of the judgment, because Elijah had foretold it. <hi type="italic">Christianos ad leones—Away with Christians to the lions.</hi> But God made them know the contrary, for the famine continued till Baal's prophets were sacrificed, and so great a scarcity of water there was that the king himself and Obadiah went in person throughout the land to seek for grass for the cattle, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.5-1Kgs.18.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Providence ordered it so, that Ahab might, with his own eyes, see how bad the consequences of this judgment were, that so he might be the better inclined to hearken to Elijah, who would direct him into the only way to put an end to it. Ahab's care was not to <hi type="italic">lose all the beasts,</hi> many being already lost; but he took no care about his soul, not to lose that; he took a deal of pains to seek grass, but none to seek the favour of God, fencing against the effect, but not enquiring how to remove the cause. The land of Judah lay close to the land of Israel, yet we find no complaint there of the want of rain; for <hi type="italic">Judah yet ruled with God, and was faithful with the saints</hi> and prophets (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.12">Hos. xi. 12</reference>), by which distinction Israel might plainly have seen the ground of God's controversy, when God <hi type="italic">caused it to rain upon one city and not upon another</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.7-Amos.4.8">Amos iv. 7, 8</reference>); but they blinded their eyes, and hardened their hearts, and would not see. <div eID="gen6916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6917" type="x-p"/> II. The steps taken towards redressing the grievance, by Elijah's appearing again upon the stage, to act as a <hi type="italic">Tishbite,</hi> a <hi type="italic">converter</hi> or <hi type="italic">reformer</hi> of Israel, for so (some think) that title of his signifies. Turn them again to the Lord God of hosts, from whom they have revolted, and all will be well quickly; this must be Elijah's doing. See <reference osisRef="Luke.1.16-Luke.1.17">Luke i. 16, 17</reference>. <div eID="gen6917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6918" type="x-p"/> 1. Ahab had made diligent search for him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.10">v. 10</reference>), had offered rewards to any one that would discover him, sent spies <hi type="italic">into every tribe and lordship</hi> of his own dominions, as some understand it, or, as others, into all the neighbouring nations and kingdoms that were in alliance with him; and, when they denied that they knew any thing of him, he would not believe them unless they swore it, and, as should seem, promised likewise upon oath that, if ever they found him among them, they would discover him and deliver him up. It should seem, he made this diligent search for him, not so much that he might punish him for what he had done in denouncing the judgment as that he might oblige him to undo it again, by recalling the sentence, because he had said it should be <hi type="italic">according to his word,</hi> having such an opinion of him as men foolishly conceive of witches (that, if they can but compel them to bless that which they have bewitched, it will be well again), or such as the king of Moab had of Balaam. I incline to this because we find, when they came together, Elijah, knowing what Ahab wanted him for, appointed him to meet him on Mount Carmel, and Ahab complied with the appointment, though Elijah took such a way to revoke the sentence and bless the land as perhaps he little thought of. <div eID="gen6918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6919" type="x-p"/> 2. God, at length, ordered Elijah to present himself to Ahab, because the time had now come when he would <hi type="italic">send rain upon the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.1">v. 1</reference>), or rather <hi type="italic">upon the land.</hi> Above two years he had lain hid with the widow at Zarephath, after he had been concealed one year by the brook Cherith; so that the third year of his sojourning there, here spoken of (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.1">v. 1</reference>), was the fourth of the famine, which lasted in all three years and six months, as we find, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.25">Luke iv. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.17">James v. 17</reference>. Such was Elijah's zeal, no doubt, against the idolatry of Baal, and such his compassion to his people, that he thought it long to be thus confined to a corner; yet he appeared not till God bade him: "<hi type="italic">Go and show thyself to Ahab,</hi> for now thy hour has come, even <hi type="italic">the time to favour Israel.</hi>" Note, It bodes well to any people when God calls his ministers out of their corners, and bids them show themselves—a sign that he will <hi type="italic">give rain on the earth;</hi> at least we may the better be content with the bread of affliction while <hi type="italic">our eyes see our teachers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.20-Isa.30.21">Isa. xxx. 20, 21</reference>. <div eID="gen6919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6920" type="x-p"/> 3. Elijah first surrendered, or rather discovered, himself to Obadiah. He knew, by the Spirit, where to meet him, and we are here told what passed between them. <div eID="gen6920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6921" type="x-p"/> (1.) Obadiah saluted him with great respect, fell on his face, and humbly asked, <hi type="italic">Art thou that my lord Elijah?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.7">v. 7</reference>. As he had shown the tenderness of a father to the sons of the prophets, so he showed the reverence of a son to this father of the prophets; and by this made it appear that he did indeed <hi type="italic">fear God greatly,</hi> that he did honour to one that was his extraordinary ambassador and had a great interest in heaven. <div eID="gen6921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6922" type="x-p"/> (2.) Elijah, in answer to him, [1.] Transfers the title of honour he gave him to Ahab: "Call him thy lord, not me;" that is a fitter title for a prince than for a prophet, <hi type="italic">who seeks not honour from men.</hi> Prophets should be called <hi type="italic">seers,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shepherds,</hi> and <hi type="italic">watchmen,</hi> and <hi type="italic">ministers,</hi> rather than <hi type="italic">lords,</hi> as those that mind duty more than dominion. [2.] He bids Obadiah go and tell the king that he is there to speak with him: <hi type="italic">Tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah</hi> is forth-coming, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.8">v. 8</reference>. He would have the king know before, that it might not be a surprise to him and that he might be sure it was the prophet's own act to present himself to him. <div eID="gen6922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6923" type="x-p"/> (3.) Obadiah begs to be excused from carrying this message to Ahab, for it might prove as much as his life was worth. [1.] He tells Elijah what great search Ahab had made for him and how much his heart was upon it to find him out, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.10">v. 10</reference>. [2.] He takes it for granted that Elijah would again withdraw (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord shall carry thee</hi> (as it is likely he had done sometimes, when Ahab thought he had been sure of him) <hi type="italic">whither I know not.</hi> See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.16">2 Kings ii. 16</reference>. He thought Elijah was not in good earnest when he bade him tell Ahab where he was, but intended only to expose the impotency of his malice; for he knew Ahab was not worthy to receive any kindness from the prophet and it was not fit that the prophet should receive any mischief from him. [3.] He is sure Ahab would be so enraged at the disappointment that he would put him to death for making a fool of him, or for not laying hands on Elijah himself, when he had him in his reach, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.12">v. 12</reference>. Tyrants and persecutors, in their passion, are often unreasonably outrageous, even towards their friends and confidants. [4.] He pleads that he did not deserve to be thus exposed, and put in peril of his life: <hi type="italic">What have I said amiss?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.9">v. 9</reference>. Nay (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">Was it not told my lord how I hid the prophets?</hi> He mentions this, not in pride or ostentation, but to convince Elijah that though he was Ahab's servant he was not in his interest, and therefore deserved not to be bantered as one of the tools of his persecution. He that had protected so many prophets, he hoped, should not have his own life hazarded by so great a prophet. <div eID="gen6923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6924" type="x-p"/> (4.) Elijah satisfied him that he might with safety deliver this message to Ahab, by assuring him, with an oath, that he would, this very day, present himself to Ahab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.15">v. 15</reference>. Let but Obadiah know that he spoke seriously and really intended it, and he will make no scruple to carry the message to Ahab. Elijah swears by <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> who has all power in his hands, and is therefore able to protect his servants against all the powers of hell and earth. <div eID="gen6924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6925" type="x-p"/> (5.) Notice is hereby soon brought to Ahab that Elijah had sent him a challenge to meet him immediately at such a place, and Ahab accepts the challenge: <hi type="italic">He went to meet Elijah,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.16">v. 16</reference>. We may suppose it was a great surprise to Ahab to hear that Elijah, whom he had so long sought and not found, was now found without seeking. He went in quest of grass, and found him from whose word, at God's mouth, he must expect rain. Yet his guilty conscience gave him little reason to hope for it, but, rather, to fear some other more dreadful judgment. Had he, by his spies, surprised Elijah, he would have triumphed over him; but, now that he was thus surprised by him, we may suppose he even trembled to look him in the face, hated him, and yet feared him, as Herod did John.
entries.251123e220486ff0aa1ac70a2baada182eabbf01: <div eID="gen6925" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Elijah's Interview with Ahab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 906.)</title> <div sID="gen6926" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And it came to pass, when Ahab saw Elijah, that Ahab said unto him, <hi type="italic">Art</hi> thou he that troubleth Israel? <hi type="super">18</hi> And he answered, I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father's house, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and thou hast followed Baalim. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now therefore send, <hi type="italic">and</hi> gather to me all Israel unto mount Carmel, and the prophets of Baal four hundred and fifty, and the prophets of the groves four hundred, which eat at Jezebel's table. <hi type="super">20</hi> So Ahab sent unto all the children of Israel, and gathered the prophets together unto mount Carmel. <div eID="gen6926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6927" type="x-p"/> We have here the meeting between Ahab and Elijah, as bad a king as ever the world was plagued with and as good a prophet as ever the church was blessed with. 1. Ahab, like himself, basely accused Elijah. He durst not strike him, remembering that Jeroboam's hand withered when it was stretched out against a prophet, but gave him bad language, which was no less an affront to him that sent him. It was a very coarse compliment with which he accosted him at the first word: <hi type="italic">Art thou he that troubleth Israel?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.17">v. 17</reference>. How unlike was this to that with which his servant Obadiah saluted him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Art thou that my lord Elijah?</hi> Obadiah feared God greatly; Ahab had sold himself to work wickedness; and both discovered their character by the manner of their address to the prophet. One may guess how people stand affected to God by observing how they stand affected to his people and ministers. Elijah now came to bring blessings to Israel, tidings of the return of the rain; yet he was thus affronted. Had it been true that he was the <hi type="italic">troubler of Israel,</hi> Ahab, as king, would have been bound to animadvert upon him. There are those who trouble Israel by their wickedness, whom the conservators of the public peace are concerned to enquire after. But it was utterly false concerning Elijah; so far was he from being an enemy to Israel's welfare that he as the stay of it, <hi type="italic">the chariots and horsemen of Israel.</hi> Note, It has been the lot of the best and most useful men to be called and counted <hi type="italic">the troublers of the land,</hi> and to be run down as public grievances. Even Christ and his apostles were thus misrepresented, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.6">Acts xvii. 6</reference>. 2. Elijah, like himself, boldly returned the charge upon the king, and proved it upon him, that he was <hi type="italic">the troubler of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.18">v. 18</reference>. Elijah is not the Achan: "<hi type="italic">I have not troubled Israel,</hi> have neither done them any wrong nor designed them any hurt." Those that procure God's judgments do the mischief, not he that merely foretels them and gives warning of them, that the nation may repent and prevent them. <hi type="italic">I would have healed Israel, but they would not be healed.</hi> Ahab is the Achan, the troubler, who follows Baalim, those accursed things. Nothing creates more trouble to a land than the impiety and profaneness of princes and their families. 3. As one having authority immediately from the King of kings, he ordered a convention of the states to be forthwith summoned to meet at Mount Carmel, where there had been an altar built to God, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.30">v. 30</reference>. Probably on that mountain they had an eminent high place, where formerly the pure worship of God had been kept up as well as it could be any where but at Jerusalem. Thither all Israel must come, to give Elijah the meeting; and the prophets of Baal who were dispersed all the country over, with those of the groves who were Jezebel's domestic chaplains, must there make their personal appearance. 4. Ahab issued out writs accordingly, for the convening of this great assembly (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.20">v. 20</reference>), either because he feared Elijah and durst not oppose him (Saul stood in awe of Samuel more than of God), or because he hoped Elijah would bless the land, and speak the word that they might have rain, and upon those terms they would be all at his beck. Those that slighted and hated his counsels would gladly be beholden to him for his prayers. Now God <hi type="italic">made those who said they were Jews and were not, but were of the synagogue of Satan, to come, and, in effect, to worship at his feet, and to know that God had loved him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>.
entries.9a85ba2ce4863de815b17f316152858c5977490b: <div eID="gen6927" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Elijah's Trial of the False Prophets; the Destruction of Baal's Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 906.)</title> <div sID="gen6928" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> God, follow him: but if Baal, <hi type="italic">then</hi> follow him. And the people answered him not a word. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then said Elijah unto the people, I, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I only, remain a prophet of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; but Baal's prophets <hi type="italic">are</hi> four hundred and fifty men. <hi type="super">23</hi> Let them therefore give us two bullocks; and let them choose one bullock for themselves, and cut it in pieces, and lay <hi type="italic">it</hi> on wood, and put no fire <hi type="italic">under:</hi> and I will dress the other bullock, and lay <hi type="italic">it</hi> on wood, and put no fire <hi type="italic">under:</hi> <hi type="super">24</hi> And call ye on the name of your gods, and I will call on the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and the God that answereth by fire, let him be God. And all the people answered and said, It is well spoken. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Elijah said unto the prophets of Baal, Choose you one bullock for yourselves, and dress <hi type="italic">it</hi> first; for ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> many; and call on the name of your gods, but put no fire <hi type="italic">under.</hi> <hi type="super">26</hi> And they took the bullock which was given them, and they dressed <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, O Baal, hear us. But <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no voice, nor any that answered. And they leaped upon the altar which was made. <hi type="super">27</hi> And it came to pass at noon, that Elijah mocked them, and said, Cry aloud: for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> a god; either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, <hi type="italic">or</hi> peradventure he sleepeth, and must be awaked. <hi type="super">28</hi> And they cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them. <hi type="super">29</hi> And it came to pass, when midday was past, and they prophesied until the <hi type="italic">time</hi> of the offering of the <hi type="italic">evening</hi> sacrifice, that <hi type="italic">there was</hi> neither voice, nor any to answer, nor any that regarded. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Elijah said unto all the people, Come near unto me. And all the people came near unto him. And he repaired the altar of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">that was</hi> broken down. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, unto whom the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came, saying, Israel shall be thy name: <hi type="super">32</hi> And with the stones he built an altar in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two measures of seed. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he put the wood in order, and cut the bullock in pieces, and laid <hi type="italic">him</hi> on the wood, and said, Fill four barrels with water, and pour <hi type="italic">it</hi> on the burnt sacrifice, and on the wood. <hi type="super">34</hi> And he said, Do <hi type="italic">it</hi> the second time. And they did <hi type="italic">it</hi> the second time. And he said, Do <hi type="italic">it</hi> the third time. And they did <hi type="italic">it</hi> the third time. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the water ran round about the altar; and he filled the trench also with water. <hi type="super">36</hi> And it came to pass at <hi type="italic">the time of</hi> the offering of the <hi type="italic">evening</hi> sacrifice, that Elijah the prophet came near, and said, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known this day that thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> God in Israel, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy servant, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> I have done all these things at thy word. <hi type="super">37</hi> Hear me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , hear me, that this people may know that thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou hast turned their heart back again. <hi type="super">38</hi> Then the fire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> fell, and consumed the burnt sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the trench. <hi type="super">39</hi> And when all the people saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> they fell on their faces: and they said, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the God; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the God. <hi type="super">40</hi> And Elijah said unto them, Take the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape. And they took them: and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and slew them there. <div eID="gen6928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6929" type="x-p"/> Ahab and the people expected that Elijah would, in this solemn assembly, <hi type="italic">bless the land,</hi> and pray for rain; but he had other work to do first. The people must be brought to repent and reform, and then they may look for the removal of the judgment, but not till then. This is the right method. God will first <hi type="italic">prepare our heart,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">cause his ear to hear,</hi> will first <hi type="italic">turn us to him,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">turn to us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Ps. x. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">lxxx. 3</reference>. Deserters must not look for God's favour till they return to their allegiance. Elijah might have looked for rain seventy times seven times, and not have seen it, if he had not thus begun his work at the right end. Three years and a half's famine would not bring them back to God. Elijah would endeavour to convince their judgments, and no doubt it was by special warrant and direction from heaven that he put the controversy between God and Baal upon a public trial. It was great condescension in God that he would suffer so plain a case to be disputed, and would permit Baal to be a competitor with him; but thus God would have every mouth to be stopped and all flesh to become silent before him. God's cause is so incontestably just that it needs not fear to have the evidences of its equity searched into and weighed. <div eID="gen6929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6930" type="x-p"/> I. Elijah reproved the people for mixing the worship of God and the worship of Baal together. Not only some Israelites worshipped God and others Baal, but the same Israelites sometimes worshipped one and sometimes the other. This he calls (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.21">v. 21</reference>) <hi type="italic">halting between two opinions,</hi> or <hi type="italic">thoughts.</hi> They worshipped God to please the prophets, but worshipped Baal to please Jezebel and curry favour at court. They thought to trim the matter, and play on both sides, as the Samaritans, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.33">2 Kings xvii. 33</reference>. Now Elijah shows them the absurdity of this. He does not insist upon their relation to Jehovah—"Is he not yours, and the God of your fathers, while Baal is the god of the Sidonians? And <hi type="italic">will a nation change their god?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jer. ii. 11</reference>. No, he waives the prescription, and enters upon the merits of the cause:—"There can be but one God, but one infinite and but one supreme: there needs but one God, one omnipotent, one all-sufficient. What occasion for addition to that which is perfect? Now if, upon trial, it appears that Baal is that one infinite omnipotent Being, that one supreme Lord and all-sufficient benefactor, you ought to renounce Jehovah and cleave to Baal only: but, if Jehovah be that one God, Baal is a cheat, and you must have no more to do with him." Note, 1. It is a very bad thing to <hi type="italic">halt between God and Baal.</hi> "In reconcilable differences (says bishop Hall) nothing more safe than indifferency both of practice and opinion; but, in cases of such necessary hostility as betwixt God and Baal, <hi type="italic">he that is not with God is against him.</hi>" Compare <reference osisRef="Mark.9.38-Mark.9.39">Mark ix. 38, 39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.30">with Matt. xxi. 30</reference>. The service of God and the service of sin, the dominion of Christ and the dominion of our lusts, these are the two thoughts which it is dangerous halting between. Those halt between them that are unresolved under their convictions, unstable and unsteady in their purposes, promise fair, but do not perform, begin well, but do not hold on, that are inconsistent with themselves, or indifferent and lukewarm in that which is good. <hi type="italic">Their heart is divided</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.2">Hos. x. 2</reference>), whereas God will have all or none. 2. We are fairly put to our choice <hi type="italic">whom we will serve,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.24.15">Josh. xxiv. 15</reference>. If we can find one that has more right to us, or will be a better master to us, than God, we may take him at our peril. God demands no more from us than he can make out a title to. To this fair proposal of the case, which Elijah here makes, the people knew not what to say: <hi type="italic">They answered him not a word.</hi> They could say nothing to justify themselves, and they would say nothing to condemn themselves, but, as people confounded, let him say what he would. <div eID="gen6930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6931" type="x-p"/> II. He proposed to bring the matter to a fair trial; and it was so much the fairer because Baal had all the external advantages on his side. The king and court were all for Baal; so was the body of the people. The managers of Baal's cause were 450 men, fat and well fed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.22">v. 22</reference>), besides 400 more, their supporters or seconds, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.19">v. 19</reference>. The manager of God's cause was but one man, lately a poor exile, hardly kept from starving; so that God's cause has nothing to support it but its own right. However, it is put to this experiment, "Let each side prepare a sacrifice, and pray to its God, and <hi type="italic">the God that answereth by fire, let him be God;</hi> if neither shall thus answer, let the people turn Atheists; if both, let them continue to <hi type="italic">halt between two.</hi>" Elijah, doubtless, had a special commission from God to put it to this test, otherwise he would have tempted God and affronted religion; but the case was extraordinary, and the judgment upon it would be of use, not only then, but in all ages. It is an instance of the courage of Elijah that he durst stand alone in the cause of God against such powers and numbers; and the issue encourages all God's witnesses and advocates never to fear the face of man. Elijah does not say, "The God that answers by <hi type="italic">water</hi>" (though that was the thing the country needed), but "that <hi type="italic">answers by fire, let him be God;</hi>" because the atonement was to be made by sacrifice, before the judgment could be removed in mercy. The God therefore that has power to pardon sin, and to signify it by consuming the sin-offering, must needs be the God that can relieve us against the calamity. He that can give fire can give rain; see <reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">Matt. ix. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.6">6</reference>. <div eID="gen6931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6932" type="x-p"/> III. The people join issue with him: <hi type="italic">It is well spoken,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.24">v. 24</reference>. They allow the proposal to be fair and unexceptionable "God has often answered by fire; if Baal cannot do so, let him be cast out for a usurper." They were very desirous to see the experiment tried, and seemed resolved to abide by the issue, whatever it should be. Those that were firm for God doubted not but it would end to his honour; those that were indifferent were willing to be determined; and Ahab and the prophets of Baal durst not oppose for fear of the people, and hoped that either <hi type="italic">they</hi> could obtain fire from heaven (though they never had yet), and the rather because, as some think, they worshipped the sun in Baal, or that <hi type="italic">Elijah</hi> could not, because not at the temple, where God was wont thus to manifest his glory. If, in this trial, they could but bring it to a drawn battle, their other advantages would give them the victory. Let it go on therefore to a trial. <div eID="gen6932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6933" type="x-p"/> IV. The prophets of Baal try first, but in vain, with their god. They covet the precedency, not only for the honour of it, but that, if they can but in the least seem to gain their point, Elijah may not be admitted to make the trial. Elijah allows it to them (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.25">v. 25</reference>), gives them the lead for their greater confusion; only, knowing that the working of Satan is with lying wonders, he takes care to prevent a fraud: Be sure to <hi type="italic">put no fire under.</hi> Now in their experiment observe, <div eID="gen6933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6934" type="x-p"/> I. How importunate and noisy the prophets of Baal were in their applications to him. They got their sacrifices ready; and we may well imagine what a noise 450 men made, when they cried as one man, and with all their might, <hi type="italic">O Baal! hear us, O Baal! answer us;</hi> as it is in the margin: and this for some hours together, longer than Diana's worshippers made their cry, <hi type="italic">Great is Diana of the Ephesians,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.19.34">Acts xix. 34</reference>. How senseless, how brutish, were they in their addresses to Baal! (1.) Like fools, <hi type="italic">they leaped upon the altar,</hi> as if they would themselves become sacrifices with their bullock; or thus they expressed their great earnestness of mind. <hi type="italic">They leaped up and down,</hi> or danced about the altar (so some): they hoped, by their dancing, to please their deity, as Herodias did Herod, and so to obtain their request. (2.) Like madmen they <hi type="italic">cut themselves in pieces with knives and lancets</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.28">v. 28</reference>) for vexation that they were not answered, or in a sort of prophetic fury, hoping to obtain the favour of their god by offering to him their own blood, when they could not obtain it with the blood of their bullock. God never required his worshippers thus to honour him; but the service of the devil, though in some instances it pleases and pampers the body, yet in other things it is really cruel to it, as in envy and drunkenness. It seems, this was the manner of the worshippers of Baal. God expressly forbade his worshippers to cut themselves, <reference osisRef="Deut.14.1">Deut. xiv. 1</reference>. He insists upon it that we mortify our lusts and corruptions; but corporeal penances and severities, such as the Papists use, which have no tendency to that, are no pleasure to him. <hi type="italic">Who has required these things at your hands?</hi> <div eID="gen6934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6935" type="x-p"/> 2. How sharp Elijah was upon them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.27">v. 27</reference>. He stood by them, and patiently heard them for so many hours praying to an idol, yet with secret indignation and disdain; and at noon, when the sun was at the hottest, and they too expecting fire (then if ever), he upbraided them with their folly; and notwithstanding the gravity of his office, and the seriousness of the work he had before him, bantered them: "<hi type="italic">Cry aloud, for he is a god,</hi> a goodly god that cannot be made to hear without all this clamour. Surely you think he is talking or meditating (as the word is) or he is pursuing some deep thoughts, (in a brown study, as we say), thinking of somewhat else and not minding his own matter, when not your credit only, but all his honour lies at stake, and his interest in Israel. His new conquest will be lost if he do not look about him quickly." Note, The worship of idols is a most ridiculous thing, and it is but justice to represent it so and expose it to scorn. This will, by no means, justify those who ridicule the worshippers of God in Christ because the worship is not performed just in their way. Baal's prophets were so far from being convinced and put to shame by the just reproach Elijah cast upon them that it made them the more violent and led them to act more ridiculously. <hi type="italic">A deceived heart had turned them aside,</hi> they <hi type="italic">could not deliver their souls</hi> by saying, <hi type="italic">Is there not a lie in our right hand?</hi> <div eID="gen6935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6936" type="x-p"/> 3. How deaf Baal was to them. Elijah did not interrupt them, but let them go on till they were tired, and quite despaired of success, which was not <hi type="italic">till the time of the evening sacrifice,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.29">v. 29</reference>. During all that time some of them prayed, while others of them prophesied, sang hymns, perhaps to the praise of Baal, or rather encouraged those that were praying to proceed, telling them that Baal would answer them at last; but there was <hi type="italic">no answer, nor any that regarded.</hi> Idols could do neither good nor evil. The prince of the power of the air, if God has permitted him, could have caused <hi type="italic">fire to come down from heaven</hi> on this occasion, and gladly would have done it for the support of his Baal. We find that the beast which deceived the world does it. <hi type="italic">He maketh fire come down from heaven in the sight of men and so deceiveth them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.13-Rev.13.14">Rev. xiii. 13, 14</reference>. But God would not suffer the devil to do it now, because the trial of his title was put on that issue by consent of parties. <div eID="gen6936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6937" type="x-p"/> V. Elijah soon obtains from his God an answer by fire. The Baalites are forced to give up their cause, and now it is Elijah's turn to produce his. Let us see if he speed better. <div eID="gen6937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6938" type="x-p"/> 1. He fitted up an altar. He would not make use of theirs, which had been polluted with their prayers to Baal, but, finding the ruins of an altar there, which had formerly been used in the service of the Lord, he chose to repair that (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.30">v. 30</reference>), to intimate to them that he was not about to introduce any new religion, but to revive the faith and worship of their fathers' God, and reduce them to their first love, their first works. He could not bring them to the altar at Jerusalem unless he could unite the two kingdoms again (which, for correction to both, God designed should not now be done), therefore, by his prophetic authority, he builds an altar on Mount Carmel, and so owns that which had formerly been built there. When we cannot carry a reformation so far as we would we must do what we can, and rather comply with some corruptions than not do our utmost towards the extirpation of Baal. He repaired this altar with <hi type="italic">twelve stones, according to the number of the twelve tribes,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.31">v. 31</reference>. Though ten of the tribes had revolted to Baal, he would look upon them as belonging to God still, by virtue of the ancient covenant with their fathers: and, though those ten were unhappily divided from the other two in civil interest, yet in the worship of the God of Israel they had communion with each other, and they twelve were one. Mention is made of God's calling their father Jacob by the name of <hi type="italic">Israel, a prince with God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.31">v. 31</reference>), to shame his degenerate seed, who worshipped a god which they saw could not hear nor answer them, and to encourage the prophet who was now to wrestle with God as Jacob did; he also shall be a prince with God. <reference osisRef="Ps.24.6">Ps. xxiv. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thy face, O Jacob!</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.12.4">Hos. xii. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">There he spoke with us.</hi> <div eID="gen6938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6939" type="x-p"/> 2. Having built his altar <hi type="italic">in the name of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.32">v. 32</reference>), by direction from him and with an eye to him, and not for his own honour, he prepared his sacrifice, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.33">v. 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">Behold the bullock and the wood; but where is the fire?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.22.7-Gen.22.8">Gen. xxii. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">God will provide himself fire.</hi> If we, in sincerity, offer our hearts to God, he will, by his grace, kindle a holy fire in them. Elijah was no priest, nor were his attendants Levites. Carmel had neither tabernacle nor temple; it was a great way distant from the ark of the testimony and the place God had chosen; this was not the altar that sanctified the gift; yet never was any sacrifice more acceptable to God than this. The particular Levitical institutions were so often dispensed with (as in the time of the Judges, Samuel's time, and now) that one would be tempted to think they were more designed for types to be fulfilled in the evangelical anti-types than for laws to be fulfilled in the strict observance of them. Their perishing thus is the using, as the apostle speaks of them (<reference osisRef="Col.3.22">Col. ii. 22</reference>), was to intimate the utter abolition of them after a little while, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.13">Heb. viii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen6939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6940" type="x-p"/> 3. He ordered abundance of water to be poured upon his altar, which he had prepared a trench for the reception of (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.32">v. 32</reference>), and, some think, made the altar hollow. Twelve barrels of water (probably sea-water, for the sea was near, and so much fresh water in this time of drought was too precious for him to be so prodigal of it), thrice four, he poured upon his sacrifice, to prevent the suspicion of any fire under (for, if there had been any, this would have put it out), and to make the expected miracle the more illustrious. <div eID="gen6940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6941" type="x-p"/> 4. He then solemnly addressed himself to God by prayer before his altar, humbly beseeching him to <hi type="italic">turn to ashes his burnt-offering</hi> (as the phrase is, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.3">Ps. xx. 3</reference>), and to testify his acceptance of it. His prayer was not long, for he used no vain repetitions, nor thought he should be <hi type="italic">heard for his much speaking;</hi> but it was very grave and composed, and showed his mind to be calm and sedate, and far from the heats and disorders that Baal's prophets were in, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.36-1Kgs.18.37">v. 36, 37</reference>. Though he was not at the <hi type="italic">place</hi> appointed, he chose the appointed <hi type="italic">time of the offering of the evening sacrifice,</hi> thereby to testify his communion with the altar at Jerusalem. Though he expected an answer by fire, yet he came near to the altar with boldness, and feared not that fire. He addressed himself to God as <hi type="italic">the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel,</hi> acting faith on God's ancient covenant, and reminding people too (for prayer may prevail) of their relation both to God and to the patriarchs. Two things he pleads here:—(1.) The glory of God: "Lord, hear me, and answer me, <hi type="italic">that it may be known</hi> (for it is now by the most denied or forgotten) <hi type="italic">that thou art God in Israel,</hi> to whom alone the homage and devotion of Israel are due, and <hi type="italic">that I am thy servant,</hi> and do all that I have done, am doing, and shall do, as thy agent, <hi type="italic">at thy word,</hi> and not to gratify any humour or passion of my own. Thou employest me; Lord, make it appear that thou dost so;" see <reference osisRef="Num.16.28-Num.16.29">Num. xvi. 28, 29</reference>. Elijah sought not his own glory but in subserviency to God's, and for his own necessary vindication. (2.) The edification of the people: "<hi type="italic">That they may know that thou art the Lord,</hi> and may experience thy grace, <hi type="italic">turning their heart,</hi> by this miracle, as a means, <hi type="italic">back again to thee,</hi> in order to thy return in a way of mercy to them." <div eID="gen6941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6942" type="x-p"/> 5. God immediately answered him by fire, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.38">v. 38</reference>. Elijah's God was neither talking nor pursuing, needed not to be either awakened or quickened; while he was yet speaking, <hi type="italic">the fire of the Lord fell,</hi> and not only, as at other times (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">Lev. ix. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.26">1 Chron. xxi. 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1">2 Chron. vii. 1</reference>) <hi type="italic">consumed the sacrifice and the wood,</hi> in token of God's acceptance of the offering, but <hi type="italic">licked up all the water in the trench,</hi> exhaling that, and drawing it up as a vapour, in order to the intended rain, which was to be the fruit of this sacrifice and prayer, more than the product of natural causes. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Ps. cxxxv. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">He causeth vapours to ascend, and maketh lightnings for the rain;</hi> for this rain he did both. As for those who fall as victims to the fire of God's wrath, no water can shelter them from it, any more than briers or thorns, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4-Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>. But this was not all; to complete the miracle, the fire consumed the <hi type="italic">stones of the altar, and</hi> the very <hi type="italic">dust,</hi> to show that it was no ordinary fire, and perhaps to intimate that, though God accepted this occasional sacrifice from this altar, yet for the future they ought to demolish all the altars on their high places, and, for their constant sacrifices, make use of that at Jerusalem only. Moses's altar and Solomon's were consecrated by the fire from heaven; but this was destroyed, because no more to be used. We may well imagine what a terror the fire struck on guilty Ahab and all the worshippers of Baal, and how they fled from it as far and as fast as they could, saying, <hi type="italic">Lest it consume us also,</hi> alluding to <reference osisRef="Num.16.34">Num. xvi. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen6942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6943" type="x-p"/> VI. What was the result of this fair trial. The prophets of Baal had failed in their proof, and could give no evidence at all to make out their pretensions on behalf of their god, but were perfectly non-suited Elijah had, by the most convincing and undeniable evidence, proved his claims on behalf of the God of Israel. And now, 1. The people, as the jury, gave in their verdict upon the trial, and they are all agreed in it; the case is so plain that they need not go from the bar to consider of their verdict or consult about it: <hi type="italic">They fell on their faces,</hi> and all, as one man, said, "<hi type="italic">Jehovah, he is the God,</hi> and not Baal; we are convinced and satisfied of it: <hi type="italic">Jehovah, he is the God</hi>" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.39">v. 39</reference>), whence, one would think, they should have inferred, "If he be the God, he shall be our God, and we will serve him only," as <reference osisRef="Josh.24.24">Josh. xxiv. 24</reference>. Some, we hope, had their hearts thus turned back, but the generality of them were convinced only, not converted, yielded to the truth of God, that he is the God, but consented not to his covenant, that he should be theirs. Blessed are those that have not seen what <hi type="italic">they</hi> saw and yet have believed and been wrought upon by it more than those that saw it. Let it for ever be looked upon as a point adjudged against all pretenders (for it was carried, upon a full hearing, against one of the most daring and threatening competitors that ever the God of Israel was affronted by) that <hi type="italic">Jehovah, he is God,</hi> God alone. 2. The prophets of Baal, as criminals, are seized, condemned, and executed, according to law, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.40">v. 40</reference>. If Jehovah be the true God, Baal is a false God, to whom these Israelites had revolted, and seduced others to the worship of him; and therefore, by the express law of God, they were to be put to death, <reference osisRef="Deut.13.1-Deut.13.11">Deut. xiii. 1-11</reference>. There needed no proof of the fact; all Israel were witnesses of it: and therefore Elijah (acting still by an extraordinary commission, which is not to be drawn into a precedent) orders them all to be slain immediately as the troublers of the land, and Ahab himself is so terrified, for the present, with the fire from heaven, that he dares not oppose it. These were the 450 prophets of Baal; the 400 prophets of the groves (who, some think, were Sidonians), though summoned (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.19">v. 19</reference>), yet, as it should seem, did not attend, and so escaped this execution, which fair escape perhaps Ahab and Jezebel thought themselves happy in; but it proved they were reserved to be the instruments of Ahab's destruction, some time after, by encouraging him to go up to Ramoth-Gilead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.6">ch. xxii. 6</reference>.
entries.3a8944a4d3d2c8b42386b1c4a715be5c08f43248: <div eID="gen6943" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Rain Sent on the Land. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 906.)</title> <div sID="gen6944" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> And Elijah said unto Ahab, Get thee up, eat and drink; for <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a sound of abundance of rain. <hi type="super">42</hi> So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Carmel; and he cast himself down upon the earth, and put his face between his knees, <hi type="super">43</hi> And said to his servant, Go up now, look toward the sea. And he went up, and looked, and said, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> nothing. And he said, Go again seven times. <hi type="super">44</hi> And it came to pass at the seventh time, that he said, Behold, there ariseth a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand. And he said, Go up, say unto Ahab, Prepare <hi type="italic">thy chariot,</hi> and get thee down, that the rain stop thee not. <hi type="super">45</hi> And it came to pass in the mean while, that the heaven was black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. And Ahab rode, and went to Jezreel. <hi type="super">46</hi> And the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was on Elijah; and he girded up his loins, and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel. <div eID="gen6944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6945" type="x-p"/> Israel being thus far reformed that they had acknowledged the Lord to be God, and had consented to the execution of Baal's prophets, that they might not seduce them any more, though this was far short of a thorough reformation, yet it was so far accepted that God thereupon opened the bottles of heaven, and poured out blessings upon his land, that very evening (as it should seem) on which they did this good work, which should have confirmed them in their reformation; see <reference osisRef="Hag.2.18-Hag.2.19">Hag. ii. 18, 19</reference>. <div eID="gen6945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6946" type="x-p"/> I. Elijah sent Ahab to <hi type="italic">eat and drink,</hi> for joy that God <hi type="italic">had now accepted his works,</hi> and that rain was coming; see <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7">Eccl. ix. 7</reference>. Ahab had continued fasting all day, either religiously, it being a day of prayer, or for want of leisure, it being a day of great expectation; but now let him <hi type="italic">eat and rink</hi> for, though others perceive no sign of it, Elijah, by faith, hears <hi type="italic">the sound of abundance of rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.41">v. 41</reference>. God reveals his secrets to his servants the prophets; and yet, without a revelation, we may foresee that when man's judgments run down like a river God's mercy will. Rain is <hi type="italic">the river of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.9">Ps. lxv. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen6946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6947" type="x-p"/> II. He himself retired to pray (for though God had promised rain, he must ask it, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zech. x. 1</reference>), and to give thanks for God's answer by fire, now hoping for an answer by water. What he said we are not told; but, 1. He withdrew to a strange place, to the <hi type="italic">top of Carmel,</hi> which was very high and very private. Hence we read of those that <hi type="italic">hide themselves in the top of Carmel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.9.3">Amos ix. 3</reference>. There he would be alone. Those who are called to appear and act in public for God must yet find time to be private with him and keep up their converse with him in solitude. There he set himself, as it were, <hi type="italic">upon his watch-tower,</hi> like the prophet, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab. ii. 1</reference>. 2. He put himself into a strange posture. He cast himself down on his knees upon the earth, in token of humility, reverence, and importunity, and <hi type="italic">put his face between his knees</hi> (that is, bowed his head so low that it touched his knees), thus abasing himself in the sense of his own meanness now that God had thus honoured him. <div eID="gen6947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6948" type="x-p"/> III. He ordered his servant to bring him notice as soon as he discerned a cloud arising out of the sea, the Mediterranean Sea, which he had a large prospect of from the top of Carmel. The sailors at this day call it <hi type="italic">Cape Carmel.</hi> Six times his servant goes to the point of the hill and sees nothing, brings no good news to his master; yet Elijah continues praying, will not be diverted so far as to go and see with his own eyes, but still sends his servant to see if he can discover any hopeful cloud, while he keeps his mind close and intent in prayer, and abides by it, as one that has taken up his father Jacob's resolution, <hi type="italic">I will not let thee go except thou bless me.</hi> Note, Though the answer of our fervent and believing supplications may not come quickly, yet we must continue instant in prayer, and not faint nor desist; for <hi type="italic">at the end it shall speak and not lie.</hi> <div eID="gen6948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6949" type="x-p"/> IV. A little cloud at length appeared, no bigger than a man's hand, which presently overspread the heavens and watered the earth, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44-1Kgs.18.45">v. 44, 45</reference>. Great blessings often arise from small beginnings, and showers of plenty from a cloud of a span long. Let us therefore never <hi type="italic">despise the day of small things,</hi> but hope and wait for great things from it. This was not as a morning cloud, which passes away (though Israel's goodness was so), but one that produced a plentiful rain (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.9">Ps. lxviii. 9</reference>), and an earnest of more. <div eID="gen6949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6950" type="x-p"/> V. Elijah hereupon hastened Ahab home, and attended him himself. Ahab rode in his chariot, at ease and in state, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.45">v. 45</reference>. Elijah ran on foot before him. If Ahab had paid the respect to Elijah that he deserved he would have taken him into his chariot, as the eunuch did Philip, that he might honour him before the elders of Israel, and confer with him further about the reformation of the kingdom. But his corruptions got the better of his convictions, and he was glad to get clear of him, as Felix of Paul, when he dismissed him, and adjourned his conference with him to a more convenient season. But, since Ahab invites him not to ride with him, he will <hi type="italic">run before him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.46">v. 46</reference>) as one of his footmen, that he may not seem to be lifted up with the great honour God had put upon him or to abate in his civil respect to his prince, though he reproved him faithfully. God's ministers should make it appear that, how great soever they look when they deliver God's message, yet they are far from affecting worldly grandeur: let them leave that to the kings of the earth.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.18"/> <div eID="gen6950" type="x-p"/>

entries.bc33e7b3305e395b2f56b750dda71c43bfe04a51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3278"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <div sID="gen4594" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.1-1Kgs.18.16">1Ki 18:1-16</reference>. Elijah Meets Obadiah.<div eID="gen4594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3278"/><hi type="bold">1. the third year--</hi>In the New Testament, it is said there was no rain "for the space of three years and six months" [Jas 5:17]. The early rain fell in our March, the latter rain in our October. Though Ahab might have at first ridiculed Elijah's announcement, yet when neither of these rains fell in their season, he was incensed against the prophet as the cause of the national judgment, and compelled him, with God's direction, to consult his safety in flight. This was six months after the king was told there would be neither dew nor rain, and from this period the three years in this passage are computed.<div eID="gen4595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Go, show thyself unto Ahab--</hi>The king had remained obdurate and impenitent. Another opportunity was to be given him of repentance, and Elijah was sent in order to declare to him the cause of the national judgment, and to promise him, on condition of his removing it, the immediate blessing of rain. <div eID="gen4596" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec3252d8ac516e85fce7ac52eaf2591747646cc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3279"/><div sID="gen4597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3279"/><hi type="bold">2. Elijah went--</hi>a marvellous proof of the natural intrepidity of this prophet, of his moral courage, and his unfaltering confidence in the protecting care of God, that he ventured to approach the presence of the raging lion.<div eID="gen4597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there was a sore famine in Samaria--</hi>Elijah found that the famine was pressing with intense severity in the capital. Corn must have been obtained for the people from Egypt or the adjoining countries, else life could not have been sustained for three years; but Ahab, with the chamberlain of his royal household, is represented as giving a personal search for pasture to his cattle. On the banks of the rivulets, grass, tender shoots of grass, might naturally be expected; but the water being dried up, the verdure would disappear. In the pastoral districts of the East it would be reckoned a most suitable occupation still for a king or chief to go at the head of such an expedition. Ranging over a large tract of country, Ahab had gone through one district, Obadiah through another. <div eID="gen4598" type="x-p"/>
entries.91de5e54003d9c7aba4f892864c604f03bd55383: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3280"/><div sID="gen4599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3280"/><hi type="bold">3. Obadiah feared the Lord greatly--</hi>Although he did not follow the course taken by the Levites and the majority of pious Israelites at that time of emigration into Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.13-2Chr.11.16">2Ch 11:13-16</reference>), he was a secret and sincere worshipper. He probably considered the violent character of the government, and his power of doing some good to the persecuted people of God as a sufficient excuse for his not going to worship in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen4599" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9ae4e59d19bfce8520d4dd0922132a1d7a818b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3281"/><div sID="gen4600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3281"/><hi type="bold">4. an hundred prophets--</hi>not men endowed with the extraordinary gifts of the prophetic office, but who were devoted to the service of God, preaching, praying, praising, &c. (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.10-1Sam.10.12">1Sa 10:10-12</reference>).<div eID="gen4600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fed them with bread and water--</hi>These articles are often used to include sustenance of any kind. As this succor must have been given them at the hazard, not only of his place, but his life, it was a strong proof of his attachment to the true religion. <div eID="gen4601" type="x-p"/>
entries.b33e0d2216f92e5e2681fe69aa0d16db154c9143: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3282"/><div sID="gen4602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3282"/><hi type="bold">7-16. Obadiah was in the way ... Elijah met him--</hi>Deeming it imprudent to rush without previous intimation into Ahab's presence, the prophet solicited Obadiah to announce his return to Ahab. The commission, with a delicate allusion to the perils he had already encountered in securing others of God's servants, was, in very touching terms, declined, as unkind and peculiarly hazardous. But Elijah having dispelled all the apprehensions entertained about the Spirit's carrying him away, Obadiah undertook to convey the prophet's message to Ahab and solicit an interview. But Ahab, bent on revenge, or impatient for the appearance of rain, went himself to meet Elijah. <div eID="gen4602" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7ab8e82abd875708fd3da8910366b6aaf32ed7b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3283"/><div sID="gen4603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3283"/><hi type="bold">17-18. Art thou he that troubleth Israel--</hi>A violent altercation took place. Ahab thought to awe him into submission, but the prophet boldly and undisguisedly told the king that the national calamity was traceable chiefly to his own and his family's patronage and practice of idolatry. But, while rebuking the sins, Elijah paid all due respect to the high rank of the offender. He urged the king to convene, by virtue of his royal mandate, a public assembly, in whose presence it might be solemnly decided which was the troubler of Israel. The appeal could not well be resisted, and Ahab, from whatever motives, consented to the proposal. God directed and overruled the issue. <div eID="gen4603" type="x-p"/>
entries.701a42a1b9dd5aca8149d4ed0af35af4dd449eb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3284"/><div sID="gen4604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3284"/><hi type="bold">19. gather ... the prophets of Baal ... the prophets of the groves--</hi>From the sequel it appears that the former only came. The latter, anticipating some evil, evaded the king's command.<div eID="gen4604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which eat at Jezebel's table--</hi>that is, not at the royal table where she herself dined, but they were maintained from her kitchen establishment (see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.25">1Sa 20:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.22">1Ki 4:22</reference>). They were the priests of Astarte, the Zidonian goddess. <div eID="gen4605" type="x-p"/>
entries.4892894b56c95dcae639ec4ab3ab225bc97a3af7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3285"/><div sID="gen4606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3285"/><hi type="bold">20. mount Carmel--</hi>is a bold, bluff promontory, which extends from the western coast of Palestine, at the bay of Acre, for many miles eastward, to the central hills of Samaria. It is a long range, presenting many summits, and intersected by a number of small ravines. The spot where the contest took place is situated at the eastern extremity, which is also the highest point of the whole ridge. It is called El-Mohhraka, "the Burning," or "the Burnt Place." No spot could have been better adapted for the thousands of Israel to have stood drawn up on those gentle slopes. The rock shoots up in an almost perpendicular wall of more than two hundred feet in height, on the side of the vale of Esdraelon. This wall made it visible over the whole plain, and from all the surrounding heights, where gazing multitudes would be stationed. <div eID="gen4606" type="x-p"/>
entries.24c99393f8089bfab7dbdc4da817f93222c607c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3286"/><div sID="gen4607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3286"/><hi type="bold">21-40. Elijah said unto all the people, How long halt ye?--</hi>They had long been attempting to conjoin the service of God with that of Baal. It was an impracticable union and the people were so struck with a sense of their own folly, or dread of the king's displeasure, that they "answered not a word." Elijah proposed to decide for them the controversy between God and Baal by an appeal, not to the authority of the law, for that would have no weight, but by a visible token from Heaven. As fire was the element over which Baal was supposed to preside, Elijah proposed that two bullocks should be slain and placed on separate altars of wood, the one for Baal, and the other for God. On whichever the fire should descend to consume it, the event should determine the true God, whom it was their duty to serve. The proposal, appearing every way reasonable, was received by the people with unanimous approval. The priests of Baal commenced the ceremony by calling on their god. In vain did they continue invoking their senseless deity from morning till noon, and from noon till evening, uttering the most piercing cries, using the most frantic gesticulations, and mingling their blood with the sacrifice. No response was heard. No fire descended. Elijah exposed their folly and imposture with the severest irony and, as the day was far advanced, commenced his operations. Inviting the people to approach and see the entire proceeding, he first repaired an old altar of God, which Jezebel had demolished. Then, having arranged the cut pieces of the bullock, he caused four barrels or jars of water to be dashed all over the altar and round in the trench. Once, twice, a third time this precaution was taken, and then, when he had offered an earnest prayer, the miraculous fire descended (<reference osisRef="Lev.9.24">Le 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.6.21">Jud 6:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.13.20">13:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.26">1Ch 21:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1">2Ch 7:1</reference>), and consumed not only the sacrifice, but the very stones of the altar. The impression on the minds of the people was that of admiration mingled with awe; and with one voice they acknowledged the supremacy of Jehovah as the true God. Taking advantage of their excited feelings, Elijah called on them to seize the priestly impostors, and by their blood fill the channel of the river (Kishon), which, in consequence of their idolatries, the drought had dried up--a direction, which, severe and relentless as it seems, it was his duty as God's minister to give (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.5">De 15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.20">18:20</reference>). The natural features of the mount exactly correspond with the details of this narrative. The conspicuous summit, 1635 feet above the sea, on which the altars were placed, presents an esplanade spacious enough for the king and the priests of Baal to stand on the one side, and Elijah on the other. It is a rocky soil, on which there is abundance of loose stones, to furnish the twelve stones of which the altar was built--a bed of thick earth, in which a trench could be dug; and yet the earth not so loose that the water poured into it would be absorbed; two hundred fifty feet beneath the altar plateau, there is a perennial fountain, which, being close to the altar of the Lord, might not have been accessible to the people; and whence, therefore, even in that season of severe drought, Elijah could procure those copious supplies of water which he poured over the altar. The distance between this spring and the site of the altar is so short, as to make it perfectly possible to go thrice thither and back again, whereas it would have been impossible once in an afternoon to fetch water from the sea [Van De Velde]. The summit is one thousand feet above the Kishon, which nowhere runs from the sea so close to the base of the mount as just beneath El-Mohhraka; so that the priests of Baal could, in a few minutes, be taken down to the brook (torrent), and slain there.<div eID="gen4607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4608" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.41-1Kgs.18.46">1Ki 18:41-46</reference>. Elijah, by Prayer, Obtains Rain. <div eID="gen4608" type="x-p"/>
entries.43dde41b105b86a839903ebae3d5a3add0b5a817: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3287"/><div sID="gen4609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3287"/><hi type="bold">42. Ahab went up to eat and to drink--</hi>Ahab, kept in painful excitement by the agonizing scene, had eaten nothing all the day. He was recommended to refresh himself without a moment's delay; and, while the king was thus occupied, the prophet, far from taking rest, was absorbed in prayer for the fulfilment of the promise (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.1">1Ki 18:1</reference>).<div eID="gen4609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put his face between his knees--</hi>a posture of earnest supplication still used. <div eID="gen4610" type="x-p"/>
entries.65788e1192206be73c7afa1729f4566fffc1b521: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3288"/><div sID="gen4611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3288"/><hi type="bold">43. Go up now, look toward the sea--</hi>From the place of worship there is a small eminence, which, on the west and northwest side, intercepts the view of the sea [Stanley; Van De Velde]. It can be ascended in a few minutes, and presents a wide prospect of the Mediterranean. Six times the servant went up, but the sky was clear--the sea tranquil. On the seventh he described the sign of approaching rain [1Ki 18:44]. <div eID="gen4611" type="x-p"/>
entries.1319e77f45525c89e59e45b959739c4e42d8ddbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3289"/><div sID="gen4612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3289"/><hi type="bold">44. Behold, there ariseth a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand--</hi>The clearness of the sky renders the smallest speck distinctly visible; and this is in Palestine the uniform precursor of rain. It rises higher and higher, and becomes larger and larger with astonishing celerity, till the whole heaven is black, and the cloud bursts in a deluge of rain.<div eID="gen4612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Prepare thy chariot, and get thee down, that the rain stop thee not--</hi>either by the river Kishon being suddenly so swollen as to be impassable, or from the deep layer of dust in the arid plain being turned into thick mud, so as to impede the wheels. <div eID="gen4613" type="x-p"/>
entries.d245f602aa71b3c2b481c651cceac06084d72fb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3290"/><div sID="gen4614" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3290"/><hi type="bold">45. Ahab rode, and went to Jezreel--</hi>now Zerin, a distance of about ten miles. This race was performed in the midst of a tempest of rain. But all rejoiced at it, as diffusing a sudden refreshment over all the land of Jezreel. <div eID="gen4614" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2aceab2648878c16ff39d5e670681c2c8ca20f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3291"/><div sID="gen4615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3291"/><hi type="bold">46. Elijah ... girded up his loins, and ran before Ahab--</hi>It was anciently, and still is in some countries of the East, customary for kings and nobles to have runners before their chariots, who are tightly girt for the purpose.
